video.title: Why Your Wrist Hurts, and How to Fix It

classification.reason: The coach gives actionable cues directing players to hit during the early stretch-release phase and maintain the wrist in an elastic support role rather than forcing it late.

problem.title_as_question: Why does your wrist hurt on the forehand, and how can you fix it?
problem.definition: Players experience wrist pain and fatigue on the forehand when trying to generate spin and power because they attempt to hit during the follow-through and actively flex their wrist to push the ball.
prerequisites: modern forehand with wrist lag and windshield wiper finish
problem.target_player: players trying to get spin and hit short-angle or high-speed forehands who hurt their wrists

symptoms.description: The hand and wrist fatigue progressively and eventually begin to hurt.
The ball fails to penetrate or travel forward when trying to strike using the late follow-through portion of the swing.
The wrist visibly moves into active forward flexion through and past contact.

causes.statement: Linear back-to-front driving racket speed peaks early and is gone after contact, transitioning entirely into rolling rotational speed.
The player's brain perceives the high rotational racket speed in the follow-through and incorrectly anchors on it as the hitting phase.
Players attempt to hit too late in the swing and must actively flex their wrist to manually drive the ball forward.
Small muscles in the hand and wrist lack the strength to actively drive a heavy racket and become overloaded when not used elastically.

angles.summary: Examines Roger Federer's forehand frame-by-frame to demonstrate that peak forward speed happens early and follow-through speed is purely rolling.
Explains that high racket head speed after contact consists of pronation and internal rotation rather than back-to-front propulsion.
Clarifies that ninety percent of the windshield wiper motion is follow-through occurring after contact rather than an active hitting movement.
Describes how players feel the high rotational velocity of the follow-through and mistakenly equate that physical sensation with ball acceleration.

solutions.summary: Think of the hitting slot as occurring earlier in the stretch-release elastic throwing phase rather than late in the swing.
Keep the wrist and hand muscles in an elastic support and release role, letting momentum transfer from big muscles rather than actively flexing to drive the racket.
Hit with the early stretch-release phase of the swing and avoid trying to drive the ball forward during the later follow-through phase.
